title: Daily Health Briefing
intro: Good morning! Today's digest spans your five tracked topics — anti-aging, HIIT for women, pelvic floor training, integrative options for HER2+/TP53 breast cancer, and sleep. Highlights: fresh human data on urolithin A for immune aging, the 48-week PEARL rapamycin results, a mid-2026 HIIT meta-analysis in women with overweight/obesity, a supervised-vs-unsupervised pelvic-floor RCT, TP53 as a possible vitamin-D biomarker in HER2+ disease, and the 2025 VA/DoD insomnia guideline. Sources are linked as chips under each section. Informational only — discuss anything you'd act on with a clinician.

sections.topic: Anti-Aging — Supplements, Rapalogs & the Hype Filter
sections.body:
This week: encouraging **human** data for **urolithin A** on immune aging, a sober look at the longest **rapamycin** trial, and a reminder that **taurine** longevity claims are still preclinical.

- **Urolithin A and "inflammaging."** A new randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (**MitoImmune, NCT05735886**) gave 50 healthy middle-aged adults **1,000 mg/day** oral urolithin A or placebo for **4 weeks**. UA expanded **naive-like, less-exhausted CD8+ T cells**, boosted their fatty-acid-oxidation capacity and mitochondrial biogenesis, and improved monocyte bacterial uptake — early evidence a mitophagy inducer can nudge the aging immune system in a favorable direction.
- **Rapamycin, longest human data (PEARL).** The decentralized **PEARL** trial tested weekly compounded **5 mg and 10 mg** rapamycin vs. placebo in adults 50–85 over **48 weeks**. The primary endpoint (**visceral fat**) did **not** change; women on 10 mg weekly showed a modest lean-tissue gain (~5%) and less self-reported pain. The reassuring signal is **safety** — adverse events and blood markers stayed comparable to placebo — but efficacy for "healthy aging" remains unproven.
- **Don't stack rapamycin with training.** The 2026 **RAPA-EX-01** RCT found once-weekly 6 mg sirolimus did **not** boost — and in sensitivity analyses may have slightly **reduced** — exercise gains in older adults.
- **Taurine reality check.** Despite heavy marketing alongside NMN and resveratrol, **human trials designed around aging endpoints are still early**; the strong data remain preclinical.

Framing: favor interventions with human RCTs, expect **modest** effects, and treat single-supplement "longevity" promises skeptically.

sections.body:
New 2025–2026 evidence keeps HIIT a **time-efficient** cardio and metabolic tool for women — best paired with **resistance/strength** work.

- **Overweight/obesity (mid-2026 meta-analysis).** A systematic review & meta-analysis of **15 RCTs** (searched through **July 2026**) in adult women with overweight, obesity, or normal-weight obesity found HIIT significantly reduced **body weight, BMI, body-fat %, and fat mass**, sharply improved **VO2max/VO2peak** (g = 1.09), raised **HDL**, and lowered **LDL** vs. no-exercise controls. Caveat: evidence certainty was rated low-to-very-low.
- **Recreationally active women.** A 2025 *Scientific Reports* meta-analysis found reliable gains in **VO2max/VO2peak** and a drop in **body-fat percentage**, but **no change in total body mass** — expect **recomposition** more than scale weight.
- **Older women (RCT).** A supervised HIIT program (3×/week) improved **aerobic capacity, lower-limb strength, and mobility (Timed Up-and-Go)**, cut body-fat and visceral-fat indices, and raised quality of life, with **no major adverse events**.
- **Postmenopausal (clinical trial, NCT07302191).** Over 12 weeks, both HIIT and **concurrent (endurance + resistance) training** improved body composition and metabolic profile; concurrent training edged out HIIT-alone for weight/BMI/%BF — a nudge to **combine intensity with strength work**.

Bottom line: intensity drives the cardio and metabolic wins; add resistance training, progress gradually, and keep recovery adequate.

sections.body:
**Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT)** remains the evidence-based **first-line** treatment for stress urinary incontinence (SUI). This week's studies converge on one theme: **supervision and correct technique matter.**

- **Supervised beats unsupervised (2026 RCT).** In 60 women with SUI, **supervised PFMT** dropped pad-test leakage from **22.89 g → 3.24 g** (p < 0.001) and got **66.7%** to Oxford grade 4–5 strength, versus a non-significant **25.71 g → 17.82 g** and only **13.3%** in the unsupervised, home-based group. Daily leak episodes fell from 7.63 → 1.69 (supervised) vs. 8.88 → 7.75 (unsupervised).
- **Prehab before surgery (Int Urogynecol J, Mar 2026).** A **6-week intensive preoperative PFMT** program in women awaiting mid-urethral sling surgery significantly improved muscle strength (Modified Oxford) and symptom severity — and **43% postponed their planned surgery** afterward, supporting structured PFMT as a low-risk step before the OR.
- **Video-guided is a good budget option.** In an urge-incontinence RCT (both arms on tolterodine), physiotherapist-**supervised** PFMT beat **video-assisted** home Kegels on symptom scores (p = 0.017), but video-assisted still improved significantly — a **cost-effective, accessible** alternative when supervision isn't available.

Key point: **confirm correct activation** (clinician or biofeedback) and stay consistent; supervised programs generally outperform unsupervised ones.

sections.topic: Integrative Options — HER2+ / TP53 Breast Cancer
sections.body:
Read "alternative" as **evidence-based integrative care alongside** standard HER2-targeted therapy — never as a replacement. Two threads stand out this week.

- **Vitamin D — and TP53 as a possible biomarker.** A 2026 *Nutrients* retrospective interventional study of curative-intent **HER2+** patients found that **failing to correct** a baseline vitamin D deficiency carried a **1.7× higher recurrence hazard**, with the best disease-free-survival trends in those reaching D25 **>50 ng/mL** (a dose-response signal). The mechanistic hook is **TP53–VDR cross-talk**: HER2+ tumors carry TP53 mutations in ~55–75%, and germline **TP53** carriers develop HER2+ disease ~67% of the time. Supporting this, an AMATERASU subset of **TP53-mutated** GI cancers saw **81% vs. 31%** 5-year relapse-free survival with vitamin D vs. placebo — hinting TP53 status may flag who benefits most.
- **Natural supplements — mechanism vs. proof.** A 2026 *Frontiers in Oncology* translational review catalogs **curcumin, withaferin A, luteolin, quercetin, and resveratrol**, noting real anti-proliferative/pro-apoptotic mechanisms but **limited robust clinical evidence**, poor **bioavailability/standardization**, and **herb–drug interaction** risk. Separately, curcumin is documented to **upregulate p53/Bax and downregulate MDM2/Bcl-2** in breast-cancer models — mechanistically interesting, but still preclinical.

Important framing: most of this is **observational or preclinical**. Use integrative options only as **oncologist-coordinated add-ons** to HER2-targeted therapy, and screen/repair vitamin D deficiency as part of standard supportive care.

sections.body:
For chronic, restless, or disjointed sleep, 2025–2026 guidance still puts **behavioral therapy ahead of pills and supplements**.

- **CBT-I is first-line (VA/DoD 2025 guideline).** The updated **VA/DoD Management of Chronic Insomnia** clinical practice guideline gives a **strong** recommendation for **CBT-I**, suggests **CBT-I over medication** as first-line, advises **against sleep-hygiene education as a stand-alone** treatment, lists the orexin antagonist **daridorexant** among newer drug options, and finds **insufficient evidence** to recommend for or against **magnesium**.
- **CBT-I wins long term.** A network meta-analysis (13 trials, ~60% women) found CBT-I produced better **long-term remission** than medication (OR 1.82; ~**41% vs. 28%**), with **fewer dropouts**, and **combination therapy was no better than CBT-I alone**.
- **Digital CBT-I works for older adults.** A 3-arm RCT of an internet CBT-I program (**SHUTi OASIS**, ages 55–95) improved insomnia severity, **sleep-onset latency, wake-after-sleep-onset, sleep efficiency, and number of awakenings** — sustained to **12 months** — useful when in-person specialists are scarce.
- **Melatonin, honestly.** The AASM recommends **against** melatonin for **chronic insomnia**; it's best reserved for **circadian problems** (jet lag, shift work).

Best-practice habits for restless/disjointed sleep:

1. Keep a **fixed wake time**, even on weekends.
2. Reserve the bed **for sleep only**; keep the room cool, dark, and quiet.
3. Dim lights and cut screens during a wind-down window.
4. If disruption persists beyond a few weeks, see a provider to rule out **sleep apnea** and consider **CBT-I** (in-person or digital).
